lessons.md:
- Offers answered what to sell; Leads answers who to sell it to and how to make them find you.

Lots of leads make it very hard to be poor — you can fail many times and still have more shots. **Advertising = making known what you have, ideally to people who don't know you yet.** Leads don't appear by magic; you force them to find you. - Alex's origin story (paraphrased): Dec 2016 he was down to ~$1,000 after a payment processor froze ~$100k.
Later, during Gym Launch's turnaround tours, one gym owner told members to refund and re-sign through him → ~$150k of refunds within a week, due in 30 days. Leila's small online coaching business suggested selling fitness direct to consumers — 48 hours writing a sales letter, ads → ~$1k/day within 14 days.
Then a gym owner who needed help asked what it would cost for Alex to just show him how (no fly-out) — Alex blurted $6k to get off the phone and the owner said yes; repeated on 7 more calls ($8k, $10k…) → ~$60k collected that day, ~$215k that month by calling past clients with the new "we'll show you how, you keep the money" model.
Lesson:
- The ability to get leads on demand = endless chances to get it right. - Trajectory he cites: Gym Launch yr1 $6.8M rev / $3M profit
- Yr2 $25.9M/~$17M
- Prestige Labs
- Yr4 ~$32M
- Sold 66% of both for $46.2M + sold ALAN
- ACQ portfolio later > $200M/yr

Tip: **document your losses early** if you expect to win.

- Problem for most businesses: **not enough leads because not enough advertising.** Solution: advertise **more, better, and in new ways** → more, cheaper, better leads from many places. All else equal, 2× leads ≈ 2× business.
- ACQ model (Alex is explicit it's not altruism, just a long time horizon): give better free products than the market's paid ones → earn trust of owners making $1M+/year profit → invest in them. Portfolio companies average ~1.8× revenue / ~3× profit after 12 months, ~2.3× revenue / ~4.7× profit after 24 months.
- **A lead = a person you can contact. An engaged lead = a person who has shown interest in what you sell** (opted in, replied, followed and can be messaged). **Engaged leads are the true output of advertising.**

- Origin: Alex's 8-week webinar flopped, but the opt-ins became calls he could close. A 13-minute screen-share **case study** ("here's how we filled a San Diego gym with 212 sign-ups: the ads, landing page, scheduler, script, results — want us to do it for you?") made leads pour in. Right lead magnet for the right avatar = huge lever. **If you don't get enough leads, the lead magnet usually isn't good or attractive enough.**
- **Definition: a lead magnet is a complete solution to a narrow problem, given away free or at a big discount, to attract ideal customers — and solving it should reveal the next problem, which only your core offer solves.** (Problem→solution cycle: every solved problem creates the next one — leads → sales → delivery → churn → ops… Business is trading bad problems for better ones.)
- Why use one: a cold audience shown only your core offer converts few; show a free narrow solution first → they pay with **time** (needs less trust than money) → you over-deliver → a higher-trust group sees the core offer → higher take rate → lower CAC. "Someone who pays with time now is more likely to pay with money later." Salty-nuts-and-water bar analogy; Costco samples drive sales.
- **9 steps**:
- **Pick the who and the narrow problem** (e.g. home sellers: what's my house worth, how to raise its value, photos, staging…).
- **Pick how to solve it — 3 types**: **reveal a problem** (diagnosis/assessment/audit — best when the problem worsens over time: site-speed audit, posture scan, termite inspection); **free trial/sample** (limit uses, quantity, time); **one step of a multi-step process** (first coat of sealant, first of 10 speed fixes, a calculator/template). Any business can use all three.
- **Pick how to deliver — 4 mechanisms**: **software/tool** (e.g. a dashboard comparing a gym's stats to industry averages — the gap is the value you can unlock), **information** (mini-course on writing ads → they then need placement, landing pages…), **services/do work free** (Alex's favourite "secret": run their ads free, get them leads, then share in the money — huge goodwill and lots of selling interface), **physical products** (book, sample, sealant bottle). 3 × 4 = 12 combinations. Keep the magnet **close to your core offer** (free branded t-shirts attract apparel buyers, not IT clients).
- **Name it** — framing decides engagement: a short video went from ~4k to ~850k views just by redoing the first 5 seconds. Alex A/B tested the book title/subtitle via polls and ads (a single word changed preference ~70/30). Test names via cheap ads (~$50), polls on every platform, comment-posts, or DMs. Winner signal: people ask when can I get it?
- **Make it easy to consume** — Alex's book consumption splits almost evenly across ebook, audio, video and print; offer every format; software on all devices; services available at more times/days; physical products simple to open and use (Apple boxes).
- **Make it good** — zero fluff; **give away the secrets, sell the implementation**; if you fear giving away your valuable thing, learn another valuable thing. **The market judges you by your free stuff** (99.9% never buy but they form opinions and tell others). People buy on a prediction of future value — the best predictor is value received before buying.
- **Create next steps — CTA**: clear, simple, direct ("be clear, not clever") + reasons to act now: **scarcity** (limited quantity) and/or **urgency** (limited time). Any reason beats no reason ("fraternity party planner" — any excuse for a party works).
- A great lead magnet: (1) ideal customers want it on sight, (2) gets more engagement than the core offer alone (lower CAC), (3) is valuable enough to actually be consumed, (4) makes the right people more likely to buy (repelling the wrong ones is fine). Great leads want great lead magnets — raise magnet quality to raise prospect quality.

lessons.t: Leads 4 — The Core Four + Warm Outreach (First 5 Clients Framework) (43 min)
lessons.md:
> **The Core Four**

= 2 audiences × 2 communication types — the only four ways one person can let others know about anything: | | Warm (they know you / gave permission) | Cold (strangers / other people's audiences) | |---|---|---| | **1-to-1 (private)** | **Warm outreach** | **Cold outreach** | | **1-to-many (public)** | **Post free content** | **Run paid ads** | - "Warm" only requires that they know you. **Outbound** = first contact happens in a private channel (call, voicemail, email, text, DM) — even an automated email blast to a list is still outbound/1-to-1.
Inbound = first contact is public (posts, ads, billboards, podcasts). **Warm outreach** — cheapest, most reliable starting point.
Alex's first business (instead of a Harvard MBA): offered free 12-week online transformations (people donated $500–1,000 to a charity) to everyone in his contacts; 6 said yes, then referrals, then they agreed to pay → ~$4k/month, replacing his consulting job. Needed only an LLC, bank account, payment method and a phone.
Steps:

# 1. Get your list
Every phone contact, email you've ever exchanged, follower on every platform (most people have 1,000–3,000). Put them in a sheet.

# 2. Pick a platform
The one with the most contacts first; reaching someone on 2 channels is almost like 2 leads; people prefer different channels.

# 3. Personalize
Spend ~30 seconds seeing what's new in their life and ask about it (people love talking about themselves).

# 4. Reach out to 100 people a day
And **follow up ~3 times** like you'd chase a friend you actually want to reach. "Everything must be hard before it can be easy."

# 5. ACA when they reply
**Acknowledge** (restate what they said — shows attention), **Compliment** (tie it to a positive trait, e.g. hard-working), **Ask** a question that steers one step closer to your offer (therapy → "do you get time for yourself?"; cleaning → "anyone help you around the house?").
Listening is value people pay therapists for.

# 6. Make the offer — to their friends, not to them
Ask if they know anyone with [problem] who wants [dream outcome] in [time]; you're taking a few free case studies (scarcity + reason why); you deliver [outcome] without [what they hate]; you guarantee it/keep working until they get it; mention 1–2 results (e.g. someone with the same struggle, someone for whom it was their first try — shows it's easy).
Most people answer "what about me?". Light ice-breaker if they say no: "anyone you don't like come to mind?".
Say it in your own words. This one message hits all four value-equation drivers.

# 7. The easiest offer
Free (for a handful) in exchange for using it, giving feedback, and leaving a review if earned. Why free first: you get reps making offers, people forgive a beginner who isn't charging, you learn faster, you collect testimonials/reviews, honest feedback, referrals.
Free customers make you money 3 ways: they convert, they refer, their testimonials sell. Thank people the moment they give feedback so they keep giving it.

- **Hinge method**: for referrals: get a **three-way intro** — in person, take their phone, start a group text with their friend and a selfie of you two; online, a group DM. Trust transfers and the friend is less likely to ghost.
- End of free period: if yes → paying client; if no → ask "what would make it worthwhile?", fix it, ask again. Uncover **hidden costs** (non-money costs — e.g. video-editing client hated recording, weekly meetings, giving feedback → use existing footage, send weekly reports, approval-only). "Just because it doesn't cost money doesn't mean it's free."
- **Repeat the list**: circumstances change (someone who wasn't ready 12 weeks ago now is).
- **Start charging**: when referrals come in or you're at capacity: 80% off for the next 5 → 60% → 40% → 20% → full price → keep raising ~20% every 5 (or 10/20) sales until you find the sweet spot. Capacity creates true scarcity and the conviction to refuse bad clients; you can even ask free clients to start paying since paying clients are waiting.
- **Pre-pay guarantee hack**: offer the guarantee only to people who pay upfront (they're more committed). After they've said yes: "would you rather pay less today, or be able to get all your money back?" — e.g. 3 × $2k with no guarantee vs $6k upfront with a guarantee; most choose upfront.
- **Keep the list warm**: mostly value, plus occasionally Dean Jackson's **nine-word email** ("Are you still looking to [desired outcome]?") → leads naturally into content.
- Checklist: who (you), what (first 5 free), where (DM/call/text/mail), **when: first 4 hours of every day**, how (personalize + ACA), **100 attempts/day**, 2 follow-ups. Benchmarks: ~80% won't reply; of 100 reach-outs expect **~1–2 buyers**; a 2,000-contact list ≈ 20–40 customers — enough to replace most incomes. "Good enough at almost anything in 20 hours; most people delay the first hour for years."

lessons.t: Leads 5 — Mozi Media Content Method Pt I: Growing an Audience (30 min)
lessons.md:
- Alex's conversion story: in 2017 his podcast had an episode arguing against branding; seeing The Rock's tequila, Conor McGregor's Proper 12 (~$600M exit), Huda Beauty, Prime, and Kylie Jenner on Forbes made him conclude he was missing **brand**. Rule he follows: anyone making more money than you has something to teach you (learning from someone ≠ becoming them). Content is a long-term asset and a **multiplier on every other kind of advertising**.
- **Content vs outreach**: outreach caps at your time (tell 10 people 10 times); content tells 10 or 10M with the same effort — more leverage but harder: you compete with everyone, and if you're good you get copied so you must keep innovating. Pros: grows your own audience (= more people you can reach out to), makes all other ads work better, costs only time, can give the highest return (a viral piece is free reach). Cons: less personal, crowded, constant innovation needed. Do one channel well first; think in years.
- **The content unit = Hook → Retain → Reward.** Every piece (even a meme) has it; long-form is many units strung together.
- **Hook** (redirect attention) with three things:
- **Topics** — far past (life lessons/behaviour changes), recent past (scan your calendar for the last week's conversations and problems), present (capture ideas in real time — Alex emailed himself, then used Twitter to test ideas daily), trending (only where you have expertise — e.g. a new tax bill for SMB owners), manufactured (stunts — he rarely does these). Best method: **do stuff and talk about what you did, repeat.**
- **Headlines** — 7 traits of high-performing news headlines (meta-analysis): **recency, relevance** (to that audience), **celebrity**, **proximity**, **conflict** (opposing ideas/values), **unusualness**, **ongoing stories**. Combine as many as you can.
- **Format** — match what has rewarded people on that platform before (the LinkedIn/Facebook/Instagram/Tinder photo meme); same video edited differently for Reels, TikTok, Shorts. A video went from ~4k to ~850k views after redoing the first 5 seconds.
- **Retain** (curiosity) with **lists** (themed items, state the number upfront — "28 ways to stay poor"), **steps** (ordered actions to a goal — less flexible, more explicit reward), **stories** (real, possible or fictional — people want to know what happens next). Interweave all three.
- **Reward** — satisfy the reason they clicked: deliver all the promised items and make them non-obvious, or they won't come back. Think **value per second**; "there's no such thing as too long, only too boring" (people binge 8-hour series). Attention spans haven't shrunk — standards have risen. Keep promises repeatedly and people start trusting your hooks on sight.
- **How you know it's good**: the audience decides; rewarding = meeting/exceeding expectations; **if your audience isn't growing, the content isn't good enough yet** (not the algorithm); practise by making more and reading feedback.
- Build skill short → long (comedians build 5-minute bits into an hour). **Make every piece for strangers** — no unexplained inside references; a 5-second "if you're new here…" doesn't bother regulars.

lessons.t: Leads 6 — Mozi Media Content Method Pt II: Monetizing Content (35 min)
lessons.md:
- **Give:ask ratio** (Gary Vee's "jab, jab, jab, right hook" — reciprocity). Goodwill is a bank account: deposit, deposit, withdraw. Signal you're doing it right: people ask you what you sell, or ask you to promote their stuff.
- Mature platforms that maximize monetization run ~**3.6–4:1** (TV ≈ 47 min content : 13 min ads per hour; Facebook ≈ 4 posts : 1 ad). Fast-growth platforms give far more (TikTok ran almost no ads for years). If you want growth, sit well on the "give" side. Alex's version: **give until they ask**; **give in public, ask in private** (reputation stays pure giving). Every public ask slows growth somewhat — fine if you need to pay bills, but make it count. If the product is exceptional, a purchase itself deposits goodwill (why he sells the book at the minimum price).
- **How to ask**: treat asks like commercials that interrupt your own value, then return to value.
- **Integrated**: a short CTA inside long content (e.g. 30 seconds in 60 minutes), ideally after a valuable moment or at the end; in writing, put CTAs in the **P.S.** (most-read part after the headline).
- **Intermittent**: for short-form — many pure-value pieces, then occasionally one piece that still hooks/retains/rewards but carries an offer (e.g. 1 in 10, 1 in 50).
- Cautionary tale: a friend's fast-growing podcast started asking too often after one lucrative ask → growth stopped, then shrank, each ask earned less.
- Ask with a **relevant lead magnet** (talking about cleaning skateboards → free cleaning guide/sample/service) whose thank-you page shows a paid offer, or with the **core offer** directly (taking a handful of people, outcome in timeframe without the pain, guarantee, DM/book/comment/reply). Books: end each chapter by pointing to free online downloads.
- **Scaling content — two routes**: **depth then width** (post on one relevant platform → post regularly → maximize quality & quantity there [short-form up to ~10/day; long-form ~weekly] → add the next platform; best when resource-constrained/new; risk = single-channel dependence) or **width then depth** (post regularly on one → add the closest platform by reformatting the same piece → cover all relevant platforms → then maximize all; broader faster but needs more skill/labour).
- **Alex's routine**: twice a month he sits down and records ~30 short clips (topics from his calendar and tweets) plus 2–4 longer videos unpacking tweets with richer stories — that alone grew ~5–6M followers in ~2 years. People overestimate time needed and underestimate how good it must be. Aim for **shareability** (platforms reward content that brings new people onto them).
- **Why it's worth it**: Gym Launch's paid ads suddenly underperformed; Leila asked what they'd stopped doing ~12 weeks earlier — Alex had stopped gym-specific content. A customer survey showed **78% had consumed at least two long-form pieces before buying** — ads were only harvesting goodwill the content built. Content also makes outreach work (prospects check your profile).
- **7 lessons**: (1) say **"how I…" instead of "how to…"** (no claim to dispute); (2) **people need reminding more than teaching** — 1 in 6 of his audience didn't know he had a book despite daily posts for two years; the Ford story (the boss was tired of an ad that hadn't launched yet) — you tire of your message long before the audience notices it; (3) **puddles → ponds → lakes → oceans** — start where you're credible (a local plumber shouldn't make general business content; talk about what you did and who you helped, which can't be questioned) and widen as credibility grows; (4) **content becomes sales tools** — reuse pieces that drive inquiries as ads, and build a "greatest hits" list mapped to objections for sales reps to send; (5) **free content retains paying customers** — people don't separate where value came from; (6) no such thing as too long, only too boring; (7) **don't pre-schedule** — manual posting gives a last quality check under immediate feedback (observed better performance).
- **First post**: it can be an announcement with an ask, because you've likely been giving for years. Alex's 2013 first post (paraphrased) announced his free-training-for-charity project, linked a site of transformations, and mentioned a few open spots — after a year of quietly doing it via DMs. Just start; ignore people who wouldn't speak at your funeral.
- **Benchmarks**: if the audience grows you did well; grows fast — better. Monthly: total followers & reach (size) and growth rate (e.g. +500 on 1,000 = 50% month). Everyone starts at zero; compare only to your past self (10 viewers is still a room of 10 people). Control inputs: pick a posting cadence and an ask cadence per platform — then start and don't stop.

Build on warm outreach first (get comfortable talking to people). Cold outreach = private 1-to-1 contact with strangers (email, call, DM, SMS, voicemail, door knocking, mail) — worked 100 years ago, works now, will work after platforms change.
Key difference from warm: **no trust**. Three new problems and their fixes:

# 1. No way to contact them → build a list
Three ways (easiest → hardest, but harder = fresher, less-bombarded lists):

- **Scrape**: with lead-scraping/outbound tools: subscribe to several, search your criteria, test a few hundred from each, buy more from the ones whose data is current, responsive and accurate.
- **Buy**: from list brokers: ask several for samples on the same criteria, test, scale with the winners, ask them for referrals to other brokers.
- **Elbow grease**: join groups/communities where your audience gathers; add qualifying members' external contact info to your list (contact them off-platform so you don't get kicked out; give more to the community than you take). **Interest groups are the warmest cold audience** — concentrated, problem-aware people already looking for a solution (scraper tools exist for them too).

# 2. They ignore you / don't trust you → personalize + give big, fast value

- Act like you know them: local area code, their name, a researched snippet about them. Generic messages get deleted.
- Rewriting all scripts to **below a 3rd-grade reading level** gave Alex ~50% more email replies.
- Strangers give you seconds — "give away the farm" with an exceptional lead magnet. Gym Launch **tripled outbound response** by offering free something competitors normally charge for (prospects already know its value). Scripts are short (first message 2–3 sentences; call script ≤1–2 pages). You learn more from 100 cold calls than 100 books.
- Pro tip: treat warm audiences with cold-outreach discipline too.

# 3. Not enough chances → increase volume

- **Automate the message**: where it doesn't hurt response: live/personal (calls, personal voice memos with their name, handwritten cards — Gary Halbert's "write as if it's your last letter") vs recorded (templated email/text, pre-recorded voicemail/video). Output = reach × response rate.
- **Automate distribution**: (dialers, blasts). Small, high-value audiences (e.g. a few thousand hedge-fund managers) → max personalization (handwritten letters, gifts); huge audiences → more automation. Tech increasingly allows both.
- **Follow up more times, more ways**: e.g. call + text + email, several times a day for the first days, then daily for a week; act like you genuinely want to reach them. After the sequence, **wait 3–6 months and work the list again** (they missed it, were busy, or circumstances changed). If someone says stop, stop — easier to turn neutral into yes than no into yes, and reputation follows you.
- New reps: **copy the best rep exactly at double the volume** until you beat their numbers — "volume negates luck"; only then experiment.
- **Voicemail trick**: "Hey [name], it's [first name] — calling in reference to [a competitor or customer they know]. Call me back at …" Short, relevant, opens a curiosity loop. Don't say "this is so-and-so from [company]"; always follow up.
- **Benchmarks**: Alex's two failed attempts at cold outreach were run by people who didn't track metrics. Example math: 100 dials → ~25% pick up → ~4 engaged leads ≈ 1 engaged lead per hour. A portfolio company's email system: ~30% open, ~10% of opens reply. Give each rep a fixed weekly lead allotment below capacity (e.g. 70 if they can handle 100) so nothing is wasted, then set absolute quotas ("70 leads → 7 appointments; no lead left behind").
- **Daily checklist**: you; hook + lead magnet or core offer with big fast value; any private channel; to scraped/bought/hand-built lists; **every day, 7 days a week; 100+ attempts/day minimum**; follow up 2–3×/day for the first days, then daily for a week; as long as it takes.
- **Why bother**: no need for content/ads or a face (works without a personality); **competitors can't see or copy it** (Alex discovered a gym company doing ~$10M/month from outbound he'd never heard of); predictable, machine-like and the pipeline stacks over time; few platform/algorithm changes; less compliance pain (only legal, not platform rules); **more sellable** business with no single rainmaker — ~50% of Gym Launch's sales came from cold outbound, a key reason for its sale multiple; scripts can last decades.
- Scale example: a portfolio company at ~$250k/month automated scraping, writing and sending — one VA sends ~2,000 emails/day → ~40 engaged leads/day → ~10% close → ~4 new customers/day, each worth $20k+ LTV — pushed them past $1M/month.

lessons.t: Leads 8 — Paid Ads Playbook Pt I: Platform, Targeting, Ad Content, Capture (47 min)
lessons.md:
- Alex says paid ads made him at least half his wealth. Story: interning near-free at a gym owner's gym (sleeping at a member's house), he learned Facebook ads at a 2-day workshop in 2013; the skeptical owner gave him $1,000 to test. His first ad was a plain text post calling out five local residents for a free 6-week challenge in exchange for before/after photos → ~19 sales at $299 (≈ $5–6k from $1k). 70–80% hit the challenge goal; then he credited their money toward a longer program. Lesson: lead-gen ads can be very simple; clarity wins.
- **How paid ads work**: you interrupt other people's content and **rent** attention from a platform. Reach is guaranteed — the only question is **efficiency** (return vs cost), never "do ads work".
- **Four problems to solve**:
- **Where to advertise** — a platform where (a) you've used it as a consumer (so your ads look like native content — the best ads blend with content; your best-performing organic content often becomes your best ad), (b) you can target your audience, (c) you know its formats, (d) you can afford the minimum spend (micro-spends democratized ads). Start with **the placements your competitors use** ("replicate before you iterate"). Use the platform's **ad library**: find the longest-running, most-engaged ads, transcribe ~50, study how they hook/retain/reward and what they offer, then write ~10 versions of your own.
- **Getting the right people to see it (targeting)** — the hardest part. Platform → narrow: start in the "puddle" (highest ROI) and widen as profits allow. Two methods, combinable: **lookalike audiences** built from your lists (best: customers; then booked calls; then opt-ins; combine warm + cold outreach lists if small) and **attribute targeting** (age, gender, income, interests, time, location). If ads underperform, the right people aren't seeing them in enough volume. **Local businesses**: the radius is already narrow — add at most one filter; local trust makes local ads the easiest ("we're next to the 7-Eleven on Fifth").
- **What the ad says** — **callout → value → call to action** (= hook/retain/reward). Never skip ads; click competitors' ads so your feed becomes a school. Each second sells the next; put ~80% of effort into the **first ~5 seconds**. Alex's method: record ~10 "meat/value" segments and ~30 hooks → ~300 variations; find the best hook, then the best meat for it.
- **Your ads aren't capped by the platform, they're capped by how good they are.** Top ~1% of Facebook advertisers test ~11× more creative and scale 10–100× further. "10 ads a month" is the real problem.
- **Callout types**: **labels** ("Clark County moms", "gym owners", "remote workers"), **yes-questions** (symptoms they nod to), **if-then statements** ("If you spend over $X/month on ads, I can cut…"), **ridiculous results** (bizarre, rare outcomes). Non-verbal callouts: **contrast** (bright colours, movement, attractive people), **likeness** (people, dress and settings that look like the avatar — lab coat for doctors, pipes for plumbers; if all your customers look like you, it's because your ads feature you), **the scene** (visualize the yes-question: someone tossing in bed; a local landmark).
- **Value — "what / who / when" framework**: What = the 8 drivers: dream outcome vs **nightmare**, likelihood vs **risk**, speed vs **slowness**, ease vs **effort** (show the good of buying and the bad of not buying; "ease comes from not needing work or skill"). Who = status from others' perspective (spouse, kids, boss, rival, colleagues — find the "key" for where they're most deprived; motivation comes from deprivation). When = past, present, future (incl. negative future: "if you keep gaining 5 lb a year…"). Combine → near-unlimited angles. Be as specific as possible within the platform's space; let visuals carry specificity.
- **CTA**: clear, not clever; one obvious action (click, call, reply yes, go to a short URL). ~80% of ACQ's traffic comes from people typing acquisition.com — Alex paid ~$370k for the domain and thinks short memorable domains are underpriced. Write for someone in a rush, below a 3rd-grade reading level.
- **Getting their contact info** — a simple **landing page**: headline + subheadline + contact form + submit (optionally an image, optionally 3 bullets). Fewer variables = faster testing and higher conversion. **Match the landing page to the ad** (same words, colours, person). More steps = fewer but better leads — add qualification if too many leads, remove if too few. Alex delayed 4 years out of tech fear, then built his first landing page in a morning.

lessons.t: Leads 9 — Paid Ads Playbook Pt II: The Money (29 min)
lessons.md:
- **What matters most: efficiency, not creativity.** All advertising "works"; the question is how well. Paid ads show return most clearly (dollars in vs dollars out per ad). You don't need the best ad ever — find ads good enough to scale and scale them hard.
- **Benchmark: lifetime gross profit (LTGP) ÷ CAC ≥ 3:1** (Alex's lifetime is ~36:1; ACQ targets ≥10:1 in portfolio companies; best ones 20:1+). Faster payback = faster compounding.
- **How much to spend — 3 phases**: (1) **track money** (no tracking = betting blind; many multi-million businesses don't know which ad works), (2) **lose money** (e.g. 10 ads × $100: nine lose, one returns 5:1 — most people quit right here; instead pour $10k into the winner), (3) **print money** (if $1 returns $10, spend as much as you can fit). Having a fixed "marketing budget" signals you don't understand paid ads — with a working machine the constraint moves to sales/delivery capacity. Expect to lose many tests; one home run pays for all.
- **Use gross profit, not revenue**: e.g. $15 product, $5 cost → $10 GP × 10 purchases = $100 LTGP. A friend's meal-prep company celebrated $100 CAC for $500 revenue customers — at 10% margins that's $50 GP, i.e. losing money. Know your margins before running ads.
- **Two levers**: lower CAC (better ads, targeting, fewer funnel steps, better sales, landing-page tests, cheaper platforms) or raise LTGP (better business model). ALAN data: CAC within an industry varied only ~1–3× between agencies; winners made ~10× more per customer. A competitor with the same sales volume as Gym Launch made ~1/56th of the profit — his problem wasn't marketing, it was value per customer. Whoever can afford the highest CAC can outbid everyone in ad auctions ("ethical monopoly") — how Gym Launch dominated.
- **Client-financed acquisition (CFA)**: the fix when LTGP > CAC but payback takes months. Example: $15/month, $10 GP, CAC $30 → 3.3:1 but cash-negative until month 3–4 (otherwise you need debt, investors or savings). Add a **$100 one-time upsell taken by 20%** → +$20 upfront → the first month covers CAC → recycle the same cash immediately (put ads on a card, pay it off, repeat), no outside capital. Making **2–3× CAC in the first 30 days** compounds (2→4→8→16…). Easiest upsells: **more, better, new** (supersize the fries, the better Coke, add fries to the burger); or simply ask customers what else would make it easier and sell that.
- **Lessons**:
- **Don't confuse sales problems with advertising problems** — a portfolio company fixed clicks, targeting, scheduling and show rate until the right people were on calls but not closing; the founder blamed ads and quit after ~$150k, "six inches from gold" — a second acquisition channel would likely have added ~$30M of enterprise value.
- **Best organic content and UGC make the best ads** — build a system for customers to send testimonial/unboxing videos, run them as ads, which brings customers who make more videos (flywheel). Content the platform already likes gets shown more as an ad.
- **Stop saying "I'm not techy"** — Alex lost 4 years to that, fixed in 4 hours.
- **Checklist**: you; offer or lead magnet; any platform where you can buy access; target/lookalike + filters; every day; get engaged leads; callout + value (what/who/when) + CTA; learning budget (track → lose → print); **if delivery is your constraint, reverse-engineer the budget** (e.g. capacity 20 new customers/month × $100 CAC = $2k/month ≈ $70/day) and fix delivery; **~30 hooks × 10 value pieces = 300 variations** on small budgets; as long as it takes (often 3–6 months click-to-close). Do paid ads after outreach/content: you'll know the avatar's language and have cash flow for a deliberate "learning budget" (e.g. expect to lose $1k/month until it clicks).

Alex's framework whenever ACQ invests in a business: **More → Better → New.**

# More
If the current advertising works, why not 10× it (100 → 1,000 cold calls/day; $1k → $10k/day ad spend)? Whatever stops you is the constraint — attack it. Often nothing is stopping you; owners are just too close to see it.

# Rule of 100
100 primary actions a day for 100 days — 100 warm reach-outs, 100 cold reach-outs, 100 minutes of content (≥1 post/day), or $100/day of ads (scale the dollars down if needed, not the effort). It's fully in your control; "4 hours a day?
Welcome to owning a small business." Doing it yourself teaches you the value of a lead and the skill to train others. Knowing how to make it rain means you'll never worry about eating.

- Top ~0.1% of Facebook advertisers test ~11× more creative; you can't scale a mediocre ad profitably. The best cold callers made more calls, the best creators made more content — do what they did.

# Better
Same effort, more leads — only via **testing**. Find the funnel step where a realistic improvement gives the biggest relative lift (e.g. opt-in 30→35% = +16%, apply 5→10% = +100%, schedule 50→55% = +10% → attack "apply"; 5→20% would 4× throughput). **Test one thing per week per channel/pathway** (clean learning, tests don't contaminate each other, forces prioritization, run to statistical significance — use an online significance calculator) → ~52 improvements a year.
Gym Launch grew ~40% after the sale doing nothing new — just quarterly targets like show rate 65→70%, CTR 1.1→1.2%, better pickup rates. **Prioritize front to back** (headline, callout, offer, CTA, landing page) — early steps have the lowest percentages and biggest returns.

- Under ~$1M profit/year: mostly do **more**. Above it, flip to **better → more → new** (percentage gains now move big numbers).

# New
New places and new ways. Fallacy: thinking a competitor on your one platform "splits the pie" — you're using one method, one platform, one audience.
Agency owner at $2M/year serving chiropractors thought he'd "tapped the market" with $40k/month of Facebook ads in a ~$10–15B industry; other chiro agencies keep getting clients, so there's more to get. Most competitors barely do anything.

- Only consider new when you've reached a meaningful share (Gym Launch talked to ~20k of ~50k US micro-gym owners via outbound — at ~20–30% penetration expand).
- Order of risk: **new placement** (same platform — stories after feed, community tab after videos) → **new platform with similar media** (short video to another short-video platform) → new platform + new media → **new Core-Four method** (hardest: e.g. paid ads → outbound team). Take half-steps and juice each one; don't pendulum-swing.
- Move to new only when more/better returns fall below what the same effort would earn elsewhere. Then run more/better on the new thing — rinse and repeat.
- Summary: advertising makes things known to strangers; lead magnets/offers convert attention into engaged leads; the Core Four are everything one person can do. Next section: getting **other people** to advertise for you.

lessons.t: Leads 11 — Lead Getters intro + Referral Playbook (47 min)
lessons.md:
- **Leverage** = output ÷ input. Not speed (going from 200 to 400 calls) — it's one action that produces 1,000 calls. Four scenarios: you get leads yourself → you train one "lead getter" (one day of work buys 365 days of theirs) → you add a lead getter every day → you hire **a lead getter who gets lead getters** (a recruiter). That's how ACQ portfolio companies get ~20k leads/day while Alex makes videos.
- **The four lead getters** (others doing the Core Four on your behalf): **customers (referrals), employees, agencies, affiliates.** The Core Four built a few million; lead getters build an empire.
- **Referral story**: two years into Gym Launch (~$500k/week), Leila noticed soft sales; Alex found every ad had been **off for two weeks** — sales only dipped from 21 to 15. First-year "100:1 ad return" was largely word of mouth. On stage before ~700 clients paying ~$42k/year, he asked who found Gym Launch through another gym owner — eventually the whole room raised their hands. $100M Offers still sells more each month than the month before with no ads.
- Referred customers have **higher LTGP, buy faster, and cost ~nothing**. Referrals are **compounding (quadratic)**, not linear. **Monthly % of customers who refer − monthly % who churn = compound growth rate.** Referrals > churn → you grow with zero advertising forever; = churn → ads needed to grow; \< churn → ads needed just to stay level ("hamster wheel of death"). Alex: he got great at advertising because he was bad at product — until his product was advertising.
- **Why businesses don't get referrals**: (1) the product isn't as good as they think, (2) they don't ask.
- **Price–value–goodwill**: goodwill = value − price (customer surplus). Price affects perceived value in both directions ($50 Chipotle burrito would feel like a rip-off; expensive wine tastes better). Big value surplus → referrers; neutral → silent; negative → haters. Raise the value ceiling so you can keep price and goodwill.
- **6 ways to give more value** (mirror the ad structure: callout → value drivers → CTA):
- **Sell better customers** — find what your top 20% have in common, filter for it in marketing and sales. Gym Launch: signed lease + ≥1 employee + ≥30 clients → results rose → marketed the better average → attracted better customers (virtuous cycle) without changing the product.
- **Set better expectations** — under-promise/over-deliver by raising real value; many readers of $100M Offers over-promised. State **factual averages** (results at month 1, 5, 12, 24) like Harvard publishing graduate incomes, not cherry-picked wins.
- **Increase likelihood of results** — survey for best results → interview what they did differently → find common actions → **force all new customers to do them** → measure → **make those actions the conditions of your guarantee** (the guarantee sells; the conditions produce results).
- **Make it faster** — "do what everyone else does in half the time"; agency that makes the phone ring right after signup vs 60-day ramp. Break big outcomes into milestones and report wins daily instead of weekly. **Choreograph the first ~28 days**; customers judge you within ~48 hours — make and keep a chain of micro-promises (email in 30 min, call from X in 2 hours, setup tomorrow, ads live the next day + notification). **BAMFAM** (from Sharran Srivatsaa): book a meeting from a meeting — never leave them in no-man's-land. Don't expect forgiveness; goodwill buys it.
- **Keep improving the product** (LTGP split-test): collect complaints → design a fix → test on struggling customers → get feedback → roll out if solved → next most common complaint, forever.
- **Tell them what to buy next** — buyers get a recurring "itch"; buying again is a top retention tool. Always show the next offer and when they'll qualify ("want us to tell you when you're ready?").
- **Thought experiment**: you lost all customers but one, and every future customer must come from that one, and any churn ends you — how would you treat them, onboard them, which customer would you choose?
- **Asking for referrals** — Dropbox (free storage for both sides → ~39× growth in ~15 months), PayPal ($10 + $10 → 1M users in ~2 years, 100M later). **7 ways**:
- **One-sided** reward ≈ your CAC (pay customers instead of the ad platforms).
- **Two-sided** — split it between referrer and friend (Alex's preference; avoids "you're just earning off me"). In Alex's service businesses ~25–30% of sign-ups came from referrals asked for **at sign-up**, which alone covered CAC. Usually 1 in 10 customers brings 10 — treat everyone the same.
- **Ask right at purchase** — names/numbers on the contract or checkout; sell it selfishly ("easiest way to double your results is doing it with a friend"); ask who, not if. A rep who simply asked "anyone you want to bring to the event?" sold 2.5× the next best rep.
- **Referrals as a negotiation chip** — instead of discounting, lower the price in exchange for introductions (ask for 3, settle for 2).
- **Referral events** (1–4 weeks, bring-a-friend challenges) — great for local businesses; they become sales events surrounded by happy customers.
- **Ongoing soft ask** woven into all content/ads ("better with a friend") — a friend saw ~33% more sign-ups (~250k of ~1M event customers referred) just by changing language.
- **Unlockable status bonuses** for people who both refer and leave a review/testimonial (VIP level, faster response, premium times, an event) — status beats cash.
- Match the incentive to what you sell (T-shirt company gives T-shirts; gift cards/credit work because they drive people back to you).
- **Killer combo — gift cards**: give every new customer a gift card worth up to ~1/3 of the price (based on gross profit, keep LTGP:CAC > 3) to pass to a friend, with a **7–14-day expiry**; have them write the friend's name on it and text a photo (three-way intro + you capture the contact); sell gift cards at ~90% off as holiday/Black Friday stocking stuffers (limit per person) — you get paid to acquire customers. Core idea: make the referrer look good to their friend.
- Referring risks the customer's goodwill with friends — they only refer when confident the friend will have a great experience. **Action**: measure referral % and churn % → apply the 6 value steps → ask with 1+ of the 7 methods.

- Story: outbound sales goal missed two quarters running. Root cause chain: need more calls → need more callers → can't hire faster than they churn → HR was doing **40 individual screening calls to hire one entry-level caller**. Switched to **group interviews** (pass people with social skills + work ethic, train the rest) → beat the goal within ~6 weeks. **Acquisition exists on both sides of the business** — scaling customer leads means scaling employee leads too.
- Lead-getting employees do the Core Four for you; a team that gets leads without you makes the business sellable. Same business ($5M revenue, $2M profit): owner working 80 h/week whose net worth is just cash vs owner working 10–20 h/week whose business is also worth $10M+ because it runs without him.
- Replace "if you want it done right, do it yourself / no one can do it like me / I'm irreplaceable" with **"if you want it done right, get someone to spend all their time on it; if I can do it, someone can do it better; everyone is replaceable, especially me."** Someone half as good who spends 100% of their time on it beats you spending 10%.
- **Recruiting = the same Core Four with different names**: warm outreach = ask your network; cold outreach = headhunting; content = posting openings/your culture; paid ads = promoted job posts. Lead getters too: customer referrals = **employee referrals**; affiliates = owners of communities of skilled people (e.g. an editors' community); employees = **in-house recruiters**; agencies = **staffing firms/headhunters**. Getting talent is advertising.
- **Training — Document, Demonstrate, Duplicate**: film yourself doing it and turn it into a checklist → do it in front of them → they do it in front of you with feedback → until they can self-correct. Entry-level ad/outreach roles need traits (grit) more than skill; **if properly trained and still below expectations ~3 weeks in, cut them** (protects team culture).
- **Calculate returns**: payroll ÷ engaged leads = cost per engaged lead (e.g. $100) × leads per customer (10) = CAC ($1,000). LTGP $40k → 4:1 — compare each lead getter to the team benchmark; show everyone the scoreboard. ACQ's media team: ~$150k/month payroll for ~30k site leads ≈ ~$3–5 per engaged lead with no ad spend. For paid ads add payroll + media.
- **Diagnosis rule**: if your CAC is >3× the industry average, ask "do my engaged leads have the problem I solve and money to spend?" — No → advertising/targeting problem; yes but too few → advertising problem; yes but not buying → **sales problem**. If you're within ~3× of the average, the issue is likely your **business model** (don't blame employees).
- **Buy vs build talent**: buying (experienced) costs more but speeds money; larger companies buy more. "Great lawyers are expensive; cheap lawyers cost a fortune." **A-players**: ~5× the output of B-players for ~25% above market — one of the biggest arbitrages in business.

- Story: early on, agencies quoted $5–10k/month he couldn't risk; a solo agency owner who "didn't sell his time" agreed to **$750/hour** to teach him. Alex drove the mouse, recorded each session, did homework; by week 6 he knew everything (≈$6k total → millions earned from that skill).
- **How agencies usually go**: best rep on your account early → good results → reassigned to win new clients → junior rep tanks results → senior pops back part-time → you cancel → next agency. (Alex rode that cycle repeatedly.)
- **How Alex uses agencies now**: only when starting something **new** (new platform or method) — to cut the learning curve. Agencies are good teachers because they must be doing what works now. Offer (paraphrased): you want to do what they do in-house; work with you ~6 months; you'll pay extra for them to explain the why behind every decision; then you'll train your team, and once your team can do it, switch to a cheaper ongoing consulting arrangement — are they open to that? Many accept; if not, the next one will. Set an internal deadline (e.g. off by month 6); expect a period of paying both. Negotiating is normal. Agencies are fine for people who never want to learn (Alex owns agency software, ALAN — he's not anti-agency).
- **Picking an agency — checklist**: (1) someone you know got results; (2) recognizable companies got results; (3) **a waiting list** (demand > supply; the best grow by word of mouth — lots of ads from small agencies is often a bad sign); (4) a sales process that sets realistic expectations; (5) **no short-term hacks** — long-term strategy with clear setup/scale/result timelines aligned with what you want (brand vs virality); (6) they say exactly what they need from you and when; (7) they propose a regular meeting cadence and multiple update channels; (8) simple reporting of cost vs results; (9) they make a good offer themselves (value equation, incl. what effort they require — make sure you can sustain it); (10) they're expensive — all good agencies are, but not all expensive ones are good.
- **Talk to 5–10 agencies** to become an informed buyer; ask liked-but-wrong-fit agencies to refer you to the best specialist they know (great referrals).
- **Next steps**: decide if an agency fits now → talk to many → use the learn-then-consult agreement → set a deadline → run both teams until yours beats theirs → drop to discounted consulting until you're teaching them → then end it. "Pay down your ignorance tax as fast as possible."

- **Prestige Labs story**: Alex's own gyms had covered all their marketing costs by upselling supplements to every new member. 3–4 years into Gym Launch he built a supplement brand plus a free "supplement selling system" for gyms (high-ticket bundles, supplement subscriptions = a second monthly paycheck per member, checklist-style iPad point of sale, **drop-shipped so gyms carried no inventory**). ~$3Minproduct+~$1M custom POS. Launch weeks 1–3: almost nothing — he did the math (5+ years to recoup) and felt like an idiot. Week 4: ~$100k+perday;weeklysalessoon~$400k+. He never sold a single supplement customer himself — **gym owners sold to their own members**. (His podcast The Game, ep. 98, captures the night before launch.) Affiliates have generated ~$50–75M lifetime across his companies.
- **Definition**: an affiliate is an independent business that tells its audience to buy your stuff — a B2B win-win, unlike a customer referral. Prestige gave gyms: upfront capital, warehousing, products they couldn't otherwise sell with no cash risk, generous commissions, simplified POS, training — and the margin let them outspend rival gyms.
- **Why an "army"**: selling 10 customers/month worth $10k each plateaus at $100k/month; selling 10 affiliates/month who each keep producing adds $100k/month **every** month — compounding nodes. Same team size to sign 1,000 gyms as 1,000 consumers, far more leverage.
- **Building it — 6 steps**:
- **Find ideal affiliates**: businesses with a warm audience full of your ideal customers — start with **warm outreach** to businesses you know. Ask: what else do my customers buy, from whom, where do they go, what do they do? D2C tip: **employers make great affiliates** (massage studio gives every new hire at a local company two free massages + a monthly lunch-and-learn).
- **Make the affiliate offer** like any ad (callout → value → CTA). Callout examples: business owner type, their customers, the result they promise, the products they deliver, or ask your own customers who owns such a business. Value template: make more from current customers / get more leads for less (dream), high likelihood (customers already want it), nothing to build/deliver/support (effort), start selling tomorrow (time). **Remove hidden costs** — do all the prep so selling is seamless.
- **Qualify/activate**: (a) **make them a customer first** (ethically try it; skin in the game — price it just high enough that they care), (b) **make them an expert** via a short certification (protects your brand from wild promises).
- **Decide what and how much to pay**: pay for the exact behaviour you want; budget = your **maximum allowable CAC** (if 3:1 is your floor, ≤1/3 of LTGP). **Three tiers** (advice from an expensive affiliate consultant the PE buyer hired — never more): tier 1 everyone (~25% of max CAC), tier 2 after an **activation** action they control (~50%), tier 3 for sustained high performance over 1–3 months (~100%). E.g. max CAC $40 on a $100 sale → $10 / $20 / $40. **Pay in product where possible** (higher perceived value, lower cost): "Sell 3, get it free" — 3+ packages/month earned a free ~$200 bundle and "sponsored athlete" status they could market. Switch to cash as volume grows.
- **Launch with Whisper → Tease → Shout**: whisper = intermittent, curiosity-only hints (movie-trailer style; Alex posting "working on book #2, version 6…" without showing it); tease = reveal the product + launch date + value elements (what/who/when); shout = high-frequency final days with bonuses, scarcity, urgency, guarantees.
- **Keep them advertising** — three integration models: (i) affiliate **gives away your lead magnet** with their product and you upsell (friend sets up free LLCs for customers of business-opportunity sellers, then upsells bookkeeping/tax and pays them a share; **white-label your lead magnets** — Alex gave gyms logo-free meal plans, grocery lists, eating-out guides); (ii) affiliate **sells your lead magnet** and keeps 100% (chiropractor's $99 posture workshop sold by gyms to desk workers, then the chiro upsells); (iii) affiliate **sells your core offer directly** (bundled or alone). Prestige uses (i) — twice-yearly national transformation challenge webinars with big prizes where gyms push members and Prestige sells — and (iii).
- **Returns**: CAC per affiliate vs gross profit of everything they bring. Example: $4k to acquire; sells $10k/month for 12 months = $120k; 75% margin → $90kGP;pay40%($36k) → $54k left → **~12.5:1**. Works at any scale (move the decimal). Low-ticket products that can't support cold outreach (a $70 lotion) can via bulk/affiliates. To improve: lower affiliate CAC (ads/offers/sales), **increase activation** (raises LTGP and lowers CAC — Alex's main focus: launch process + tiers), improve the long-term integration model.
- **Two ways to build a compounding business**: people who never stop buying (customers for life — Coca-Cola) or people who never stop selling for you (affiliates). Referrals are the first, affiliates the second; you need one of them to build something massive. Treat affiliates like customers — they are a different tier of customer.
- **Action**: advertise the affiliate offer until you have **10–20 affiliates** → get them results and fix offer/terms/launch/integration from their feedback → turn their results and marketing into lead magnets for recruiting more affiliates → scale.

lessons.t: Leads 15 — Open to Goal / Execution (18 min)
lessons.md:
- **Learning budget** story (June 2017, ~4 months after losing everything): Alex paid $10k to attend a private event for 8-figure owners. A speaker doing ~$30M/year said he no longer learns much from courses; instead he sets aside a fixed slice of ad spend (e.g. 5–10%) for crazy ideas with **full permission to fail** — most do nothing, occasionally one reinvents the market. Alex set a fixed **$10k/month learning budget** and scaled harder: ~$1M → $1.2M → $1.5M → $2.5M → $4M/month (and ~$16M/month across ACQ later). ACQ's media team runs monthly "hackathon" days for wild content ideas; outreach teams change a script/offer ~10% of the time. Keeps you innovating and prevents burnout.
- **Flyer lesson**: Alex put out 300 flyers, got one angry call (scratched Mercedes), declared flyers dead. His mentor tested in batches of **5,000** (0.5% ok, 1% good, 2% killing it) and ran **~5,000/day (~150k/month)** — ~500× Alex's volume. Vow: never let effort be the reason something didn't work. Most strategies work with enough volume.
- **Rule of 100 = baseline** ("your duty to yourself"). **Open to Goal = Rule of 100 on steroids**: set an outcome target and don't stop until you hit it, however long it takes (a 15-location gym chain run by an ex-football coach let sales managers leave only once the daily sales goal was hit; a top door-knocker counted out loud until 20 appointments). Builds a different muscle. "What's required is greater than your best" — your best has to improve.
- **How Alex structures the day**: wake early for **4–6 uninterrupted hours** (or late night — the point is uninterrupted deep work); **no rituals** — coffee and straight to work (a long routine must justify itself vs just working); **no meetings before noon** (5am–noon = a full extra work week each week); newer hack: **schedule meetings back-to-front** (pile them at the end of the day) to protect ~10 uninterrupted hours. When it feels like too much: this is where most people stop.
- **One-page execution plan**: (1) pick the engaged-lead type (customers, affiliates, employees, agencies); (2) pick Rule of 100 or Open to Goal and commit to daily actions (100 reach-outs / 100 minutes content / a set ad spend or learning budget) — bonus: an extra 100 of another Core Four activity; (3) fill the checklist: who (you), what (offer/lead magnet), where (platform), to whom (audience/list), when (first 6–8 hours), why (X leads or lead getters), how (which Core Four), how much (100 or until goal), how many follow-ups, how long (100 days or until goal); (4) repeat daily until you can afford to pay someone to do it; (5) then make employees your target lead type and repeat until you have the help you need. If you're not doing the Core Four enough, it's your fault — and your responsibility, which is power.

1. ---

- **Friends know** — one offer, one avatar, one platform; warm outreach.
2. **Everyone you know, consistently** — you know the inputs that produce an engaged lead; max your personal capacity (Alex: paid ads with a case-study lead magnet; he wishes he'd started content earlier) — warm outreach + content.
3. **Employees advertise for you** — you've maxed your own inputs, not the platform; hire people to advertise profitably (Alex hired a videographer and a media buyer).
4. **Product good enough for consistent referrals** — aim for **≥25% of customers from referrals**; go back and improve the MVP before scaling further, or you enter the hamster wheel and damage your brand. "Go slow to go fast" (advice from a Broadcom COO mentor).
5. **More places, more ways, more people** — new audiences on your best platform → all placements/media types there → then another platform, lead getter or Core Four activity; profitable on **≥2 methods across multiple platforms**.
6. **Hire killers** — battle-hardened executives/department heads who've already done exactly this, with strong outcome incentives. For marketing, **years of relevant experience > age**. Alex's cold outreach failed with an external consultant, failed with an internal hire without experience, worked with an internal hire with experience. If you're teaching them in the interview, wrong hire — you should be learning from them.
7. (Beyond $1B — Alex says he'll report back when he gets there.)
8. The full machine: media team scaling content everywhere; regular offers to the audience; an audience that makes any launch profitable; teams scaling paid ads on many platforms; a cold outreach team bringing more customers than you can handle; an affiliate manager launching new affiliates daily; recruiters bringing in more lead getters; a product so good ~1/3 of customers bring more; an exec team driving growth without you.

lessons.t: Leads 17 — Recap & the many-sided die (12 min)
lessons.md:
- Recap: lead → engaged lead → lead magnet/offer → Core Four → More/Better/New → four lead getters → Rule of 100 / Open to Goal → 7 levels.

# Parable (summarized)
Two players each roll a die with one green side among many red ones (one has far more sides than the other), and each green turns another side green. The one who keeps rolling eventually rolls green more and more often; the one who complains about the other's "luck" and quits loses.
You never know whether someone is on their 100th or 100,000th roll. Two guarantees: the more you roll, the better you get; and if you quit, you lose.
Alex's mantra on hard days: **you cannot lose if you do not quit.** Even after years, he expects to lose more ad tests than he wins.

- Free goodies mentioned: a bonus "finding your avatar" chapter (acquisition.com/avatar), next book on sales/persuasion, ACQ careers, investment for companies with $1M+ profit. Proof of skill transfer: Alex's best gym did ~$600k/year — today the average Gym Launch gym does more. Closing motto: per aspera ad astra (through hardships to the stars).

## Lead Generation & Advertising

265 ideas from 108 videos. [#N] = video N in the Start here tab.

- Calling leads within five minutes can roughly triple sales; implement CRM, round-robin and call prioritization even though it is boring. [▶ 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RdAKXJlMIZM)
- If ad costs rise faster than impression costs, you likely have negative word of mouth; fix the product before scaling marketing. [▶ 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RdAKXJlMIZM)
- Eight ways to advertise: the core four you do yourself (warm outreach, content, cold outreach, paid ads) and four lead getters who do them for you (customer referrals, employees, agencies, affiliates). Pick one to start, and founders should personally learn marketing and sales first. [▶ 2](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VBoRLJimVzc)
- Nobody knows you exist: even with a huge book launch, almost nobody he met had heard of it. Repeat your core messages constantly (people need reminding more than teaching), and early on follow the "4x4": four hours a day on the core four, guided by the rule of 100 (100 minutes of content, 100 outreaches, or $100/day in ads). [▶ 6](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oRMG_HpOAN4)
- Getting the first five customers via warm outreach: greet, give a specific compliment, insert your one-liner, and ask if they know anyone who could benefit; do this four hours a day or 100 messages a day until five customers come in. [▶ 14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nIk3DedjxJM)
- Control what people say about you by giving them simple words to describe your business; e.g. he planned to shift Acquisition.com's mission wording to "make real business education available to everyone" because the original phrasing was too abstract to repeat. [▶ 16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cq8GyLrEuAk)
- Under $1M in revenue, assume nobody knows you exist: spend the first four hours of every day on one of the core four (warm/cold outreach, content, ads). Advertising is an order-of-magnitude lever (he calls it a "BOOM"), while conversion tweaks are capped at 100%; a gym needing 200 members in a city of 1M people needs only a tiny fraction of the market, so competitors barely matter. [▶ 17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HxEQCHpZzHk)
- Clear, not clever: write at a 3rd-5th grade reading level (rewriting follow-up emails to that level lifted conversion about 50%), use analogies from the audience's world (cars for mechanics, houses for realtors) and universal experiences for broad audiences. [▶ 17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HxEQCHpZzHk)
- Steal from yourself: put about 70% of effort into copying what works, 20% into adjacent variations (same hook, new setting), and 10% into new ideas; most people do the reverse, and customers tire of a winner long after you do. [▶ 17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HxEQCHpZzHk)
- Marketing laws: state the facts and tell the truth, change reality to make the truth compelling, show and say what only you can (one of six rare black belts nationally, "it's toasted"), and be the best in a small puddle (Rockefeller overpaid to become the biggest refiner, then consolidated about 20 rivals within 30 days). [▶ 17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HxEQCHpZzHk)
- Targeting comes first: a great coat offer fails if shown to Florida. Make the person in the ad look like the avatar (putting Leila's photo on a thank-you page sharply raised responses and show-ups). Masters track more leading indicators (time to fill, cost to acquire talent, 90-day fit; in outbound: list quality, data enrichment, pickup rates, hook, offer, show rate) instead of binary outcomes.
